content: We have Finset.min which has the option of Top, and if you know your finset is nonempty, you can use Finset.min' which returns the original type. I'm surprised we don't have a Finset.min'' which, assuming the Type HasZero, returns the junk value 0 instead of Top. Is this something we'd like to have in Mathlib?
When I needed this, I chained Finset.min with WithTop.untopD
Yes, isn't that ugly, if it needs to be used repeatedly?
But that's if there's already OrderTop in the Type...
docs#List.head! uses the default value of the type (from Inhabited) as junk value. So maybe Finset.min!?
The version which returns an Option could be Finset.min? if we want to follow that pattern.

I don't think I personally would mess with Finset.min? (though maybe that's a pattern we want to continue? Including Finset.inf? etc) But I like the idea of Finset.min! -- should we add it, and some API around it?
If you're convinced it's useful for you then why not! Why do you (think you) need it?
Because I didn't think that .min.untopD 0 looked as nice, and was surprised we didn't already have it. (See: Zaremba's Conjecture)
I think you can also sInf (s : Set ℕ) which will give zero when your Finset is empty (docs#Nat.sInf_empty)
For that context, is letting the return value be in WithTop Nat not more natural?

Oh and since you're using Finset.image beforehand, you can also do

iInf fun a : coprimeResidues d ↦ maxPartialQuotient a d

Both sInf and iInf make the def noncomputable... As for the return value being WithTop ℕ, that's actually what it (implicitly) was the first time around; then it made the clean statement of the conjecture (∃ A, ∀ d, minmaxPartialQuotient d ≤ A) either trivially true (setting A = Top) or, if changed to ∃ (A : ℕ), ∀ d, minmaxPartialQuotient d ≤ A, it's false because for d = 0, minmax = Top. So I'd have to change the statement to the much uglier ∃ (A : ℕ), ∀ d ≥ 1, minmaxPartialQuotient d ≤ A, and I'd rather add Finset.min!..?
I think ∃ (A : ℕ), ∀ d ≥ 1, minmaxPartialQuotient d ≤ A is probably the better spelling here, since it avoids the reader having to check whether the junk values make the statement uninteresting

The game you're playing is "let's try to make a statement where the junk values happen to work out so that it's still interesting", but that makes the formalization further from the informal question. For mathlib of course this kind of behavior is encouraged to make lemmas maximally useful, but for formal-conjectures what matter is making the statement maximally reflective of the underlying question.
